title: Life Cycle of Stars
keyIdea: Stars are born in nebulae, huge clouds of gas and dust. Gravity pulls the gas together until the core is hot enough (about 15 million °C) for hydrogen to fuse into helium, which makes the star shine; it is not burning like a fire. A star shines for millions or billions of years while it fuses hydrogen: the Sun will last about 10 billion years and is about halfway. Heavier stars have more fuel but use it much faster, so they live shorter lives. When the core hydrogen runs out, a star like the Sun swells into a red giant, puffs off its outer layers and leaves a white dwarf that slowly fades. A star more than about 8 times the Sun's mass swells into a red supergiant and explodes as a supernova, leaving a neutron star or a black hole, and its scattered gas and dust can form new stars and planets.
familyTip: On a clear night, look for Betelgeuse, the reddish star at Orion's shoulder: it is a red supergiant that will one day explode as a supernova. Then compare it with blue-white Rigel at Orion's foot. Ask: which ending will each star have, and why does a star's mass decide it?

visual.caption: Which ending does each star or stage belong to? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: squeeze a nebula into a star, run the Sun's hydrogen clock, rank star lifetimes, build both endings, sort stars by mass.

kid: Stars are born in a nebula. A nebula is a huge cloud of gas and dust in space. Gravity pulls the gas together. The middle gets hotter and hotter.
When the core reaches about 15 million °C, hydrogen starts to fuse into helium. This gives out heat and light, and a star is born. A star is not on fire. It shines by fusion.
A star shines while it has hydrogen to fuse. Our Sun will shine for about 10 billion years. It is about halfway now. Big stars have more fuel, but they use it much faster. So big stars die young.

When the hydrogen runs out, the star swells up. A star like the Sun becomes a red giant. Its outside drifts away, and a small white dwarf is left to fade. A star more than about 8 times heavier than the Sun becomes a red supergiant. Then it explodes in a supernova.
adult: Ages 9 to 11. In the National Curriculum in England, Year 5 Earth and space describes the Sun as a star. This lesson follows the topic's own evidence: stars form from nebulae, make energy by fusing hydrogen into helium in their cores, and end as white dwarfs or, if massive, in supernovae. It previews the GCSE Physics space topic (AQA 4.8.1.2, the life cycle of a star), which uses the same stages.

Key facts used. Gravity pulls the gas in and heats the core. Fusion starts at about 15 million °C, the temperature of the Sun's core. The Sun is about 4.6 billion years old and will fuse hydrogen for about 10 billion years in all. Heavier stars live much shorter lives, because their brightness rises far faster than their fuel. A star of 10 solar masses lasts about 20 to 30 million years. Small red dwarfs last hundreds of billions of years or more. Stars below about 8 solar masses become red giants and then white dwarfs; the shed layers form a planetary nebula. Heavier stars become red supergiants, explode as supernovae and leave neutron stars or black holes. The scattered elements later form new stars and planets.

Common mistakes: thinking stars burn like a fire (they fuse nuclei, with no oxygen involved); thinking more fuel means a longer life; thinking every star ends in a supernova, including the Sun; muddling a nebula (where stars begin) with a black hole (one possible end); and calling a planetary nebula a planet. The lab makes each of these a prediction or a challenge option.

choices: a huge cloud of gas and dust where stars form
practice.hint: Think of where a star begins its life.
practice.explain: A nebula is a cloud of gas and dust. Gravity pulls parts of it together to make new stars.

practice.prompt: A star lives for about 10 billion years. It is now {a} billion years old. About how many billion years does it have left?
practice.hint: Take its age away from its whole life.
practice.explain: 10 − {a} = {=10-a} billion years left before its core hydrogen runs out.

practice.prompt: Which star will have the shortest life?
choices: a blue giant, 10 times the Sun's mass
practice.hint: Heavy stars have more fuel, but how fast do they use it?
practice.explain: Heavy stars burn their fuel much faster, so the blue giant lives only tens of millions of years.

practice.prompt: Stars more than about 8 times the Sun's mass explode as supernovae. A star is {m} times the Sun's mass. How many times the Sun's mass is it above that limit?
practice.hint: Take 8 away from the star's mass.
practice.explain: {m} − 8 = {=m-8}, so it is above the limit and will end in a supernova.

choices: hydrogen fusing into helium in its core
practice.hint: Stars make their own light. How?
practice.explain: In the hot core, hydrogen nuclei fuse into helium and give out energy. There is no fire.

pool.prompt: How will the Sun end its life?
choices: as a red giant, then a white dwarf
pool.hint: Is the Sun more or less than 8 times its own mass? It is exactly 1.
pool.explain: The Sun is too light to explode. It will swell into a red giant, shed its outer layers and leave a white dwarf.

pool.prompt: A star is 25 times the Sun's mass. What comes after it swells into a red supergiant?
choices: it shrinks back to a nebula
pool.hint: Stars over about 8 Suns end with a bang.
pool.explain: A star this heavy explodes as a supernova, leaving a neutron star or a black hole.

pool.prompt: What pulls a nebula together to start a star?
pool.hint: It is the force that pulls masses towards each other.
pool.explain: Gravity pulls the gas and dust inwards. Squeezing makes the core hotter until fusion starts.

pool.prompt: A star like the Sun fuses hydrogen for about {t} billion years. How old is it when it is halfway through, in billions of years?
pool.hint: Halfway means half of the whole time: divide by 2.
pool.explain: {t} ÷ 2 = {=t/2} billion years. The Sun, at about 4.6 billion years, is close to halfway through its 10 billion.

pool.prompt: Why does a star 10 times heavier than the Sun live a shorter life?
choices: it uses its fuel much faster
pool.hint: It has more fuel, so the answer is about speed.
pool.explain: Heavy stars are far brighter and fuse hydrogen much faster, so they run out first.

pool.prompt: What can a supernova leave behind?
choices: a neutron star or a black hole
a new Sun the same size
pool.hint: Think of the heaviest stars' path.
pool.explain: The core of the exploded star is crushed into a neutron star or, if heavy enough, a black hole.

pool.prompt: Put these in order for a star like the Sun: white dwarf, nebula, red giant, shining star.
choices: nebula, shining star, red giant, white dwarf
shining star, nebula, white dwarf, red giant
red giant, nebula, shining star, white dwarf
pool.hint: Start where all stars start: in a cloud.
pool.explain: Nebula → shining (main-sequence) star → red giant → white dwarf.

pool.prompt: A star's core hydrogen will last {t} billion years in all. After {u} billion years, how many billion years are left?
pool.hint: Take the time used away from the whole time.
pool.explain: {t} − {u} = {=t-u} billion years left before it swells up.
